about.heading: Trinity
about.introParagraph: Environment, humanity, and machine are often understood as separate forces, yet each continuously shapes and transforms the others. Trinity gathers these three forces—Environment, Human, and Machine—not as independent subjects but as an interconnected system in which each shapes, produces, and transforms the others. The environment gives form to human life; humanity extracts, reshapes, and reorganizes its materials to create machines; and machines return to transform both their creators and the environment from which they originated. This relationship is not linear but cyclical: environment shapes humanity, humanity creates machinery, and machinery continuously reconstructs the conditions of both. Rather than resolving these tensions, the exhibition asks what happens when environment, humanity, and machine can no longer be understood independently—together forming a system that continuously creates, consumes, adapts, and transforms itself.
pressParagraphs: New York, NY — A Space Virtual Gallery is pleased to present Trinity, a group exhibition in virtual space that examines the relationship between environment, humanity, and machine. The show brings together works across painting, sculpture, film, video, animation, net art, photography, and mixed media, moving through creation and destruction, the organic and the artificial, embodiment and invisibility, control and autonomy, extraction and regeneration.

Rather than treating environment, humanity, and machine as separate subjects, Trinity considers them as a single cyclical system: environment shapes humanity, humanity creates machinery, and machinery continuously reconstructs the conditions of both human and environmental existence. The works gathered here examine the connections, conflicts, and dependencies within this three-part structure.

Ely Taylor’s rust I and silent spring I picture autonomous war machines rusting into ponds and cannons riddled with arrows, weapons and nature outlasting the humanity that built them, while the divine feminine and femina ex machina turn that cycle of destruction and regeneration inward, rendering transition as an act of transformation and quiet letting go. Brian Gray’s MEMO and In Medias Res treat celluloid itself as a living material, each viewing altering the film through improvised synthesizer performance and live stereoscopic projection. Ben Moren’s Birch Transducer (veery) turns a hollow of birch bark into a speaker membrane, letting a decaying fragment of forest echo the migratory birdsong recorded within it.

Johanna Spieker’s cambrian_explosion_2.0 borrows the language of sudden biological diversification to describe the accelerating development of AI, professing love for CGI while mourning the moral fragility of digital space. Tereza Vinklárková’s Scab unfolds inside a memory-erasing machine, an experimental video essay that reads addiction as a mechanism of regulation, dissociation, and escape. Lucas Megson’s Two--Fold and Carolina Bash paint the staged violence of southern wrestling culture, where real and fake personas collide as entertainment and spectacle.

Víctor Armando Mancilla Ríos’s Snakes and Dungeons opens an interactive menu of links, doors, and windows where the twin themes of war and love clash on the game board of the world. Jack Conti’s Let’s get ready explores human dependency through automated processes, laser-cut and inkjet-printed onto acrylic. Bianca Rotunno’s R.E.M loops through chrome dreams of machine, environment, and humanity, uneasy about which weight the cycle finally bends toward. Areesha Ahmed’s TheToxicSludge_ pulls a social-media account back into physical form—collage mounted on wood and packed with hot glue—insisting that something human survives the platform’s machinery of extraction.
Together, the works trace a system in which environment, humanity, and machine can no longer be separated—continuously creating, consuming, adapting, and transforming one another.

currentShow.title: rust I
currentShow.medium: Gouache and alcohol marker on cold-pressed watercolor block
currentShow.description: rust I depicts an autonomous war machine that has fallen out of use, outlasting humanity and the war it was originally designed for. The machine has sunk into a pond where it has since rusted over and now feeds the local ecosystem, covered in lichens, barnacles, and mosses, taking on a new life after its first. While mankind is no longer present to witness this new turn of the cycle, its legacy lives on through the machines it created which in turn decay to give life to the local flora.

currentShow.title: silent spring I
currentShow.medium: Gouache and alcohol marker on cold-pressed watercolor block
currentShow.description: silent spring I depicts an armed cannon riddled with arrows, having fallen in some unnamed battle. The title of the piece references Rachel Carson’s book of the same name which helped to shed light on the potential long-lasting impacts of synthetic pesticide use on the environment and the dangers it posed to life as a whole. In this piece, mankind has already fallen to a war of its own making, its weapons and nature itself outlasting humanity.

currentShow.title: the divine feminine
currentShow.description: The divine feminine is the first in a two-part series made as I was coming to terms with the fact that I am trans. This piece depicts the post-transition version of me killing the pre-transition version of me, while still holding her gently with love and forgiveness. The piece is less about an act of violence and moreso one of transformation and letting go of the things that hold you back in order to become your ideal self.

currentShow.title: femina ex machina
currentShow.medium: Acrylic and cyanotype ink on canvas
currentShow.description: Femina ex machina is the second piece in this two-part series, made a few months into my medical and social transition. Around this time, I began to feel incredibly isolated by my transition, and made this piece to reflect on and depict some of the hardships and joys that transitioning had brought me. Through creating this piece, I was able to find solace in the path I had chosen.

currentShow.title: MEMO
currentShow.description: This work is a materialist expression of contemporary existential anxiety. Each viewing is singular in that it significantly alters the celluloid and it's manipulations to a substantial degree and is accompanied by an improvised modular synthesizer performance.

currentShow.title: In Medias Res
currentShow.description: In Medias Res is a live stereoscopic projection event that employs shadow-play, live animation, and experimental projection techniques in an attempts to immerse the viewer deeply in impossible spaces and landscapes. Mechanized puppetry, video feedback and expanded cinema performances are displayed in anaglyphic 3D, working from techniques developed by the American Experimental Cinema pioneer Ken Jacobs.

currentShow.title: Birch Transducer (veery)
currentShow.medium: Birch hollow, field recording, audio transducer, custom electronics, brass
currentShow.description: A transducer converts energy from one form to another. Here, an audio voice coil excites the birch bark hollow, transforming it into a speaker membrane. Inspired by the haunting, descending call of the Veery, a migratory bird bridging Boreal/Mixed Hardwood and Amazon forests; Field recordings capture a chorus of forest dwellers: Swainson's Thrush, Magnolia Warbler, Cedar Waxwing, Black-and-white Warbler, Ovenbird, Black-throated Green Warbler, White-throated Sparrow, Red-eyed Vireo, Veery, Common Yellowthroat, Canada Warbler, Black-capped Chickadee, American Robin, Downy Woodpecker, Nashville Warbler, Red-winged Blackbird, and Pileated Woodpecker. Once still and quiet, the Birch bark now echoes the intricate harmonies of its environment.

currentShow.title: cambrian_explosion_2.0
currentShow.description: (The term, referring to the rapid diversification of life forms (c. 538.8 Ma), is now being used to describe the accelerated development of AI.) With this work, I express my love for technology and CGI, while lamenting the corruption and moral fragility of tech and digital spaces. Post Production: Richard Lu Jia Wellershoff. Voice: Johanna Kahlcke. Mixing and Mastering: Jonas Meyburg. Song: “Everything Stays” – written and composed by Rebecca Sugar, from Adventure Time. Software: Blender, Substance Painter, Visual Studio Code, Topaz Labs, DaVinci Resolve, Native Instruments, Reaper

currentShow.title: Scab
currentShow.description: Strup begins with a detective searching for clues in stories that may not belong to the person telling them. Set inside a memory-erasing machine, the experimental video essay explores addiction as a complex mechanism of emotional regulation and escape. Blurring the boundaries between substance use, dissociation, fantasy, and memory manipulation, Strup draws on optogenetic research into the alteration of memory.

currentShow.title: Two--Fold
currentShow.description: This work is exploring the connection between violence and materialism, specifically in southern culture. Wrestling as a form of entertainment blurs the lines between theater and sport. There is an amalgamation of real and fake violence as well as real and fake personas that are put on display for the audience to take in. Peacocking and flashiness are coupled with this complex display of violence which intertwines these two ideas. This particular subject is only one example of the way that this phenomena can manifest in popular culture and American society. My work is centered around these themes of which I try to explore through my own lens of personal experience.

currentShow.title: Snakes and Dungeons
currentShow.description: “Snakes and Dungeons” is an interactive menu featuring projects created in 2026; it consists of a series of links, doors, windows, and interactive spaces hosted on a webpage—designed to be accessed via mobile phone or computer. All these links articulate, in one way or another, one or both of the two core themes of this moment and this generation: war and love. These two themes clash on the game board known as the world, intersecting within my own body to produce the "body" of work I present here. I invite you to share a few minutes of *extimacy*.

currentShow.title: R.E.M
currentShow.description: Thick chrome dreams are flooding the land. Is the curdle of electrified meat swimming in cushioning waters resilient enough? Is it resilient like the hills and ocean depths or is it soft and malleable like light transmitting fibers?

currentShow.title: TheToxicSludge_
currentShow.medium: Collage made on Instagram Create Mode, Wooden Tray, Hot Glue, Pebbles, Heart-Shaped Bell
currentShow.description: I built an account under the handle @thetoxicsludge_ to hold everything at once — memes, ideas, the smallest parts of an ordinary day — and watched it become something closer to an environment than a profile: its own weather, its own residents, its own rules for what got to survive. The platform is a kind of machine, and like any machine, it doesn't just hold what you put in — it reshapes you. What felt private got pulled outward, sorted, made visible or invisible by an algorithm deciding what was worth seeing. A playground started to function like a battlefield. Turning the account into a physical object — mounting the collage on wood, packing it with hot glue — was an attempt to pull something back from that cycle. Glue and wood don't scroll away, and take real time and real pain to shape by hand. If the platform extracted a version of me and resold it as image, this object is the regeneration side of that same loop: something organic pushing back against something built to consume it. It doesn't undo the extraction. It just insists something human survives it.
